description:
## What
fps-tnz (PR for branch claude/fps-tnz-353bc6) fixed a floating-point bug in `_noise_band`
(experiments/pipeline/dossier_tables.py): `np.std(deltas) > 0` alone doesn't catch "every
draw landed on the same value" because np.std of many identical floats (e.g. twenty 0.01s)
is ~1.78e-18, not exactly 0.0, due to binary float rounding. The fix pairs it with
`np.ptp(deltas) > 0` (exact, zero iff draws are truly identical) — matching a guard
`_comparable_noise_banks` already used (PR #345, fps-30p).

The identical bug PATTERN (`np.std(...) == 0` or `np.std(...) > 0` used as an "is this
effectively constant" gate, without the ptp exactness pairing) recurs uncorrected in:

- fuel_signal/shap_report.py:91 — `if len(v) < 2 or np.std(v) == 0 or np.std(s) == 0:`
  gates Pearson r for the feature-summary table (PRODUCTION code, runs on every SHAP report)
- fuel_signal/shap_report.py:130 — same pattern gating the SHAP interaction-score sum
- experiments/shap_phase4/rank_partners.py:51 — verbatim copy of the shap_report.py:130 loop
- experiments/shap_phase4/lga_shap_plots.py:68 — same guard before computing r for LGA plots
- experiments/shap_phase4/dependence_grid.py:84 — same guard for the dependence-grid r column

## Why I noticed this
Surfaced by the altitude angle of a code review of the fps-tnz diff — the fix was correctly
generalized within dossier_tables.py (matches its sibling function) but the same failure
family exists elsewhere, including in production code, not just experiments/.

## Failure scenario
A near-constant sample (e.g. large-magnitude values differing only in the last few bits
after a shared-offset subtraction) can produce `np.std() ≈ 1e-13`, not exact 0. The `== 0`
guards then miss it entirely, and `np.corrcoef` divides by that near-zero std, producing a
spurious/inflated `r` (or NaN from 0/0) instead of the intended "undefined, skip" behavior.

## Files likely affected
- fuel_signal/shap_report.py
- experiments/shap_phase4/rank_partners.py
- experiments/shap_phase4/lga_shap_plots.py
- experiments/shap_phase4/dependence_grid.py

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the 5 sites pairs its std-based degeneracy check with an exact `np.ptp(...) == 0`
      (or `> 0`) check, consistent with `_comparable_noise_banks`/`_noise_band`
- [ ] Consider extracting a shared helper (e.g. `_is_constant(arr)`) given the pattern now
      appears in 3+ places — dossier_tables.py already has TWO near-verbatim inline copies
title: Apply ptp-exactness fix to std==0 degeneracy checks outside dossier_tables.py

description:
## What

`fuel_signal/fill.py` sets `MAX_GAP_FILL_DAYS = 28`: a station's daily price series is
forward-filled across gaps of 28 days or less, and gaps longer than that are left
unfilled entirely. `labels.py` then requires 90 contiguous lookback days and 7
contiguous forward days, so it strips a further 7 rows before and 90 after any
surviving hole.

Compounded, **the minimum possible hole in the modelling frame is 28 + 7 + 90 = 125
days**. Observed minimum across all 245 holes in the batch1 frame: exactly 125. Median
132. A station that goes unreported for one month disappears from the model for four
and a half.

The cap was introduced deliberately in 87bd867 (2026-05-11) to exclude closed/rebuilt
stations: *"preventing stale prices from polluting label computation and cycle
detection during station closures/rebuilds"*. That rationale is sound. The defect is
that the rule cannot tell a **closure** from a **source-data outage** — both present
as one long gap — and it silently chose the wrong answer for 81 stations in March 2022
(see fps-tpy).

## Why this matters

- 245 holes across 198 of 714 stations; 38,833 missing station-days in the batch1 frame.
- Removal is silent. Nothing in the pipeline reports that ~12% of the panel vanished.
- It fires hardest exactly when the source feed is degraded, which is when the frame is
  already weakest.

## Proposed fix

A genuine closure is **idiosyncratic** — one station dark while the panel reports
normally. A source outage is **synchronised** — a large fraction of the panel is
missing the same dates. The current rule ignores that signal, and no threshold on
`MAX_GAP_FILL_DAYS` can recover it.

So gate the cap on concurrency:

- For a candidate gap on station S spanning `[a,b]`, measure the fraction of the panel
  that also has no observation across `[a,b]`.
- High fraction (source outage): fill through it regardless of length — the station was
  demonstrably trading; we just were not told the price.
- Low fraction (real closure): keep the current 28-day refusal.

**Open design question, needs a decision:** filling through a 19-day publication hole
carries a stale price across a window in which the market moved 15-20 c/L. That may be
worse than exclusion *for labels*. A likely compromise is to fill for panel-membership
and aggregate purposes (so the station keeps feeding `network_px_std`,
`lga_mean_cents`, `brand_mean_cents` and does not vanish for four months) while leaving
**labels** unset across the affected span. Decide before implementing.

## Files likely affected

- `fuel_signal/fill.py` (`MAX_GAP_FILL_DAYS`, `find_daily_gaps`, `fill_all`)
- `fuel_signal/labels.py` (contiguity requirements at lines ~151/162, ~232)
- `tests/test_fill.py`

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Gap handling distinguishes synchronised (panel-wide) from idiosyncratic gaps
- [ ] Decision recorded on the fill-vs-label split above, with its rationale
- [ ] Pipeline reports panel-membership changes rather than dropping stations silently
- [ ] Test covers: idiosyncratic long gap (still excluded); synchronised long gap
      (filled); the 125-day compounding no longer occurs for the synchronised case
- [ ] Re-measure the March 2022 cohort: 81 stations should stop vanishing for 4+ months

## Trail

Full investigation, including two retracted hypotheses (stale DB; genuine price
plateau), is in this issue's comments. Split out of the original composition-drift
framing on 2026-08-25.
notes:
## Third case the concurrency fix would NOT catch (found 2026-08-26, dossier review)

The proposed fix classifies gaps as synchronised (source outage → fill through) vs
idiosyncratic (real closure → keep the 28-day refusal). There is a third case that is
idiosyncratic but NOT a closure, and concurrency would send it down the wrong branch:

**A live station that simply reports too infrequently.**

Evidence, verified against data/cleaned/ raw prices:

- Stations 414 (BP Springwood, suburb Valley Heights) and 18517 (Shell Blaxland) are
  both DARK in features.parquet across 2021-08-07..2022-02-06 (184 days).
- Only 2 of 718 stations share that span — textbook "idiosyncratic", so the proposed
  concurrency gate keeps the 28-day refusal and still drops them.
- But raw prices EXIST inside the gap: 414 has 44 rows, 18517 has 75. Neither closed.
  Their update rate simply fell to ~1/3 of prior (414: ~27-32/month before, 5-10 after),
  which is sparse enough for consecutive single-fuel updates to exceed 28 days.

**The discriminator is simpler and stronger than concurrency:** do raw rows exist
inside the candidate gap at all? If yes, the station was demonstrably trading —
regardless of whether the gap is synchronised. Concurrency is a proxy for that; raw-row
presence is the thing itself. Suggest gating on raw-row presence first, then using
concurrency only for the fill-vs-label decision already flagged as an open question.

## Related sub-defect: the label tail overruns a genuine reopening

Station 414's 2022-08-25..2023-10-17 gap IS a real closure (a year-long rebuild;
zero raw rows 2022-09..2023-04, confirmed by the owner). But it reopened ~2023-07 and
was actively reporting (19/37/33/32 rows in Jul/Aug/Sep/Oct 2023) while the feature
frame stayed dark until 2023-10-17 — ~3 months of pure labels.py 90-day strip applied
after the station was demonstrably back. Actual closure ~8 months; data loss 419 days.

Impact seen in batch1: all 607 extra_feature_provider_misses in every batch1 candidate
run trace to these two stations, confined to folds 1-8. Fold 1 loses 2 of 5 preferred
stations for all 90 days (neither closed), and fold 8 loses 82/90 for 414 on
label-strip tail alone. See experiments/candidates/batch1/lga_trough_propagation/README.md
§ Review addendum.
title: fill.py's 28-day gap cap cannot distinguish a station closure from a source-data outage

close_reason: Fixed by fps-3jj.21. `candidate_pool`'s fallback tail no longer restarts the seed cycle at index 0 — seeds now come off `placebo.block_seed(i)`, an unbounded flat counter that never wraps, so no two picks in a bank can share a block order. Verified on the batch1 frozen frame with the shipped code: a 20-draw arity-3 bank has 60/60 distinct seeds and a worst cross-draw placebo correlation of 0.350 (the between-station floor pair station_minus_lga_mean_cents/stickiness_score, an already-named limitation of the construction), against 0.965 in the committed 10-draw ruler. All three of this bead's acceptance criteria are met; the behaviour change it flagged (a recomputed arity-1 floor differs from a committed one once substitution fires) is recorded in docs/CONVENTIONS.md. Measurement: experiments/2026-08-26_placebo_draw_independence/.
description:
## What

`placebo.candidate_pool`'s fallback tail cycles `PLACEBO_BLOCK_SEED_POOL` from index 0,
so as soon as a primary candidate is substituted away, a later draw reuses an earlier
draw's block seed. Same seed = same block permutation ORDER, so if the two draws' SOURCE
columns are correlated, their placebo columns are correlated too — and the draws are not
independent, which is the one property the band's std assumes.

Fix: start the fallback tail's seed cycle at `len(primary)` instead of 0, so a substitute
never collides with a primary.

## Measured, not hypothesised (2026-08-23, batch1 frozen frame)

Arity-3 bank, 10 draws x 3 columns. Within-draw correlation is fine everywhere (worst
0.348, well under the 0.85 the redundancy screen uses). The problem is ACROSS draws:

    0.965   d1 cycle_pct_through@97   <->  d10 cycle_days_since_peak@97
    0.778   d1 cycle_mean_length@101  <->  d10 cycle_last_min_cents@101

Both pairs share a seed, and their sources are the lock's most-correlated pair
(cycle_pct_through vs cycle_days_since_peak sit at 0.971 — the same quantity in two
units). So draws 1 and 10 are near-duplicates: the bank has ~9 independent draws, not 10.

batch1's committed ARITY-1 floor has the same defect — seeds 97 and 101 each appear
twice, after two all-NaN LGA primaries were substituted.

## Why this is P3 and not a blocker for fps-3jj.14

The defect predates arity and affects BOTH sides of the arity comparison (k=1 and k=3
floors alike), so it largely cancels in the k=3/k=1 std ratio that comparison turns on.
`family_wise_z_threshold` already takes `n_draws` into its t degrees of freedom, so the
cost of ~9 effective draws instead of 10 is a marginally optimistic bar, not a wrong one.

## Note before fixing

This CHANGES what a recomputed arity-1 floor produces, so it is not a free refactor:
- it breaks fps-3jj.14's deliberate "arity 1 is byte-identical" property for FUTURE runs
  (committed floors on disk are untouched — nothing recomputes them);
- `tests/test_placebo.py` and `tests/test_noise_floor.py` both assert seed behaviour and
  will need updating alongside;
- any floor recomputed after this lands is not comparable to one computed before it,
  so it wants the same treatment as a re-lock: recompute, don't mix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Fallback-tail seeds never collide with primaries
- [ ] The measurement above re-run: no cross-draw placebo pair above ~0.5 on batch1
- [ ] Tests updated, and the behaviour change called out in docs/CONVENTIONS.md
title: Placebo draws can share a block seed, making two draws non-independent

description:
## What

A candidate blocked by `validate.py`'s target-column guard (`TargetColumnInInputs`, or a
`COLUMNS` collision with the label columns) lands in `STATUS_ABORTED_CANDIDATE` — the
same bucket as a missing output column, an all-NaN column, a bad INPUTS declaration, or
any exception `add_columns` throws. `STATUS_DISQUALIFIED` exists and is unused for this.

The taxonomy as written supports `aborted_candidate`, so this is not a defect. The
question is whether it should be `disqualified` instead, so that "the generator proposed
an oracle feature" is separable from "the generator wrote code that crashed".

## Why it matters

fps-3jj's aim (b) is stated as gaining experience with an AI-sourced pipeline —
explicitly including **"how often it produces leaky or redundant candidates"**. That is a
rate, and a rate needs its numerator to be distinguishable. Right now the retrospective
(fps-3jj.8) cannot compute it: every leak is pooled with every ordinary bug.

Not urgent — batch1 has to actually run before there is anything to count, and if the
guard is doing its job the count may well be zero. But if it is nonzero and we cannot
tell, we lose the single most interesting datapoint the batch could produce about the
generator.

## Options

1. Map the target-column refusals to `STATUS_DISQUALIFIED`; leave everything else at
   `aborted_candidate`. Check `TERMINAL_STATUSES` / dossier + retrospective handling.
2. Keep the status and add a structured `abort_reason` code to `results.json`, letting
   the retrospective count without re-cutting the status taxonomy.

(2) is probably better — it generalises to redundancy and PIT aborts, which have the same
problem.

## Context

Raised as a "not sure" item in the external review of PR #325 (fps-3jj.12); intent was
never stated in the bead, so it is a decision, not an oversight.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide (1) vs (2) vs leave-as-is, and record why
- [ ] If changed: retrospective can report a leak/abort breakdown per batch
title: Leak-by-declaration is invisible in the outcome taxonomy — aim (b) wants a leak rate

description:
## What

`_dry_audit` lives in `experiments/2026-08-20_cadence_ceiling/model_cadence.py` (fps-fii).
`experiments/2026-08-21_tau_cadence/tau_sweep.py` (fps-929) is its SECOND use and imports
it by file path via `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location`, which works but means one
experiment now imports another experiment's script as a library.

## Why now

This repo's stated rule is to hoist shared glue into `experiments/lib` on second use
(cf. `fps-1785999729817-2`, the external-series realised-arbiter glue, filed on the same
trigger). Second use is reached.

The audit is also the kind of code that must not be transcribed twice: its correctness
rests on mirroring `run_backtest`'s own level arithmetic exactly (on a BUY the engine
sets level to full and charges `size - level`; on an emergency it sets level to half and
charges `0.5*size - level`, so post-fill level is `level + litres` in both cases). A
second copy is a second chance to get that subtly wrong, silently — the failure mode is
a cell that has silently bought fewer litres than the arms it is compared against.

## Files

- from: `experiments/2026-08-20_cadence_ceiling/model_cadence.py` (`_dry_audit`, `DRY_TOL`)
- to:   `experiments/lib/` (new module, or an existing one if a natural home exists)
- callers: `model_cadence.py`, `experiments/2026-08-21_tau_cadence/tau_sweep.py`

## Notes

`DRY_TOL` travels with it and its rationale must travel too — it is deliberately a
PHYSICAL quantity (1 mL) rather than a float epsilon, because an epsilon-scale threshold
does not separate genuine dry events (>= 3.571 L even at the finest cadence swept) from
the ~1.7e-6 L/step replay drift that `run_oracle_backtest`'s per-layer 6dp rounding
produces. See the comment block in `model_cadence.py` before moving it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_dry_audit` + `DRY_TOL` in `experiments/lib`, with the DRY_TOL rationale comment intact
- [ ] Both callers import it from there; the importlib-by-path hack in `tau_sweep.py` removed
- [ ] fps-fii's and fps-929's published dry-audit numbers reproduce unchanged
title: Hoist _dry_audit into experiments/lib (second use reached)

description:
## What fuel_signal/tgp.py currently sources the AIP TGP series exclusively from the weekly xlsx (fps-8qc). That file is only refreshed on Fridays (confirmed across 4 consecutive weeks in Aug 2026 — see fps-8qc), so data_lag_days climbs from 0 right after a Friday refresh to 6 by the following Thursday. http://api.aip.com.au/public/tgpTables serves an HTML page (not JSON, despite the api. subdomain and clean path) with a rolling 5-weekday-column table per capital city, refreshed more often — confirmed live 2026-08-20 to have data through Tuesday 18 Aug, i.e. ~1-2 days lag vs. the xlsx's 6. ## Why I noticed this User asked whether the xlsx's several-day-old "current" data was expected, which led to characterising the weekly cadence (fps-8qc PR discussion, 2026-08-20). This endpoint was the second URL candidate the user suggested when the original job broke, but the xlsx source turned out to still be functional post-URL-fix, so this is deliberately scoped as a lag-reduction enhancement, not a replacement. ## What the endpoint actually looks like - Plain HTTP (no TLS) — `http://api.aip.com.au/public/tgpTables`. - Server-rendered HTML: a `` per fuel type (first is headed "Petrol (ULP, cents per litre, inclusive of GST)"). - Column headers carry explicit dates, e.g. `Wednesday
12 August 2026`, so parsing does not need to infer dates from "today" — same robustness property as the xlsx. - Row headers are city names; Sydney's `` has `href="http://api.aip.com.au/public/sydneyUlp"` for identification. - Only ever shows 5 columns (current rolling weekday window) — no deep history, so this cannot replace the xlsx backfill, only extend its tail. ## Shape of the work - Add an HTML-table parser (BeautifulSoup, same dependency already used for the xlsx landing-page scrape) alongside the existing xlsx path in fuel_signal/tgp.py — most likely: fetch both, and let the tgpTables rows (by date) override/extend the xlsx-derived series for the tail where they overlap, before write_series_csv(). - Decide whether this changes the "single source of truth = the full-history xlsx" storage rationale documented in tgp.py's module docstring (#271) — the tgpTables data would only ever cover the last ~5 weekdays, so the xlsx stays authoritative for anything older; this is purely about reducing tail lag. - Update the module docstring + the tgp-fetch.yml cron comment (which currently references this issue as the tracked lag-reduction path) once landed. ## Files likely affected - fuel_signal/tgp.py - tests/test_tgp.py - .github/workflows/tgp-fetch.yml (comment currently points here) ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] New parser for the tgpTables HTML endpoint, unit tested against a saved fixture - [ ] Sydney tail series extended with tgpTables data where fresher than the xlsx, without discarding xlsx history - [ ] data_lag_days logging reflects the improved (tgpTables-backed) lag, not just the xlsx's - [ ] docstring + workflow comment updated to describe the two-source design
title: Pull TGP data from api.aip.com.au/public/tgpTables (1-2 day lag) alongside weekly xlsx

description:
## What

Build a diagnostic that answers "does the model mistime its buys in regime X?" as a
RATE rather than a cost: for each decision the model made, did it choose a worse week
than the oracle did? Tag the decision by its regime and compare rates across regimes.

## Why — it sidesteps an identification problem, it isn't a workaround for one

fps-1785999730023-4-264564ac established that per-zone headroom (model_cpl -
oracle_cpl sliced by cycle zone) is **not identified**: it depends on two free
bookkeeping conventions with no physical content — cost basis (fifo/average: which
litre you burn first) and interval label (start/mid/end: which date stamps a burn
spanning [d, d+7)) — and across those 6 combinations each zone moves further than the
zones differ from each other. No amount of extra data fixes that; it is a bias term,
not variance.

The root cause is specific: allocating a **path-coupled total cost** across
sub-periods has no unique answer. A rate has no such problem. A decision happened at a
moment; it was better or worse than the alternative; nothing is spread over time.
All three conventions vanish rather than being averaged over.

## Why it is also lower variance

The cost measure is dominated by how far prices happened to move — within-fold spread
of price paid is 8.03 c/L, giving SE ~0.72 c/L on ~124 chosen late-descent decisions,
against a between-regime effect around 0.5 c/L. The error is bigger than the signal.

A yes/no rate over the same 124 decisions gives roughly +/-4.5 percentage points, which
resolves a 10-point difference between regimes comfortably. Same data, far less noise,
because the price-swing magnitude that was drowning the signal is discarded.

## Design notes

- Pair at the DECISION, not the zone: for each model decision date, what did the
  oracle do in the same tank state / same window? Define "worse week" carefully —
  the oracle's own fill dates are the reference.
- Report the rate AND the conditional cost (given a mistime, how much did it cost?).
  Rate is the detector; cost is the sizer. Same screen-then-arbiter shape used
  elsewhere in this repo. Do not let the cost half sneak per-zone allocation back in
  — condition on the decision, not on the period.
- Emergency fills are NOT decisions (66% of model fills, 51% of oracle). Exclude them
  from the rate denominator; they belong to the consequences of earlier decisions.
- Sample size is now the live constraint again, unlike for headroom, because this IS
  a variance-limited measure. More stations genuinely help here — see the stratified
  sampling notes on fps-x0f (sample evenly across LGA trough-lag bands rather than
  proportionally: an even spread sharpens the slope, proportional sharpens the
  Sydney-wide average, and the slope is what we want).

## Files likely affected

- experiments/<date>_decision_timing/ (new)
- possibly a helper in experiments/lib/ if the pairing proves reusable (2nd-use rule)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Per-regime rate of "model chose a worse week than the oracle", with CIs, emergency fills excluded
- [ ] Conditional cost given a mistime, reported separately from the rate
- [ ] Explicit demonstration that the measure is invariant to the cost-basis and interval-label conventions that killed the headroom decomposition
- [ ] A verdict on fps-x0f step 2: is late descent measurably worse than normal?
- [ ] Result recorded in ledger.yaml + INDEX.md whichever way it lands

## Related

- fps-x0f — this replaces its step 2; that issue should depend on this one
- fps-1785999730023-4-264564ac (closed) — the identification finding this responds to
title: Decision-timing accuracy: a zone diagnostic that never allocates cost to a period

description:
## What

Two questions, in order. The second is the interesting one; the first has to be
answered before the second can mean anything.

1. **Is "late descent" a measurable soft spot at all?** Three findings on that axis
   disagree, and all three are cut on an axis with a known, unfixed defect.
2. **Does `station_minus_tgp_cents` (the TGP gap) help on late-descent rows?** Never
   tested. It was rejected on the SHOCK axis, which is not the axis its mechanism
   targets.

## Why — the three disagreeing findings

| measurement | baseline compared against | late descent | normal | reads as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gate 1 layer-1 (regret proxy, 2026-06-18) | oracle ceiling, cheap proxy | 1.72 | 1.05 | **worst** zone |
| Gate 1 layer-2 (realised saving%, 2026-06-18) | regime-matched always-buy | 2.13% | 0.64% | **better** than normal |
| Headroom map #262 (2026-06-19) | oracle ceiling, realised | 1.00 | 1.50 | **least** recoverable |

Rows 1 and 3 both claim to measure distance-from-oracle and give opposite orderings.
Row 2 uses always-buy, a weak baseline, so it measures value DELIVERED not value
AVAILABLE — it can look strong while headroom is untouched.

Row 3 is the one that RESTED the late-descent thread ("regime axis FLAT ->
independent confirmation of #259"). If it is wrong, that thread was closed on a bad
reading.

## Why — the axis those three are cut on is defective

All three slice on `cycle_pct_through` = `days_since_last_peak / mean_cycle_length`.

`_mean_cycle_length` (fuel_signal/cycle.py:270) is an unweighted average over ALL
confirmed peaks to date — still the expanding all-history mean:

    days_between_peaks = np.diff(cycle_times) ...
    return float(round(np.average(days_between_peaks), 2))

This is defect 2 from the parked 2026-06-14 corner_oracle_sweep. It was never fixed:
the 2026-06-16 regime_cycle_length experiment tested a regime-local replacement,
found it genuinely MORE ACCURATE (~27d -> 38d, removing ~1.15x fold-7-era inflation),
and abandoned it because it did not buy realised value. So the accuracy problem is
untouched — the denominator still lags the early-2020 ~24d -> ~38d regime shift,
inflating the phase axis ~13% (worse in fold 7's era).

Consequence: the "late descent" band boundary is systematically misplaced. Rows are
labelled late-descent when they are not, and vice versa. Every one of the three
findings above is a measurement taken through that lens.

Note the 2026-06-16 abandonment is NOT evidence the axis is fine. It showed a more
accurate denominator does not improve CPL when used AS A MODEL FEATURE (the
"accuracy != objective" lesson). That says nothing about whether it is fit for use as
an ANALYSIS AXIS for segmenting rows, which is what all three findings use it for.
Those are different jobs and the abandonment only tested one of them.

## Why — the TGP result that was never converted

June's oracle diagnostic (experiments/2026-06-20_leading_indicators/) measured:

- gap -> depth-remaining  r2 = **0.63**
- gap -> days-remaining   r2 = 0.47
- gap / slope             r2 = 0.19  (worse — "ship raw gap not the time projection")

r2=0.63 is a strong existence result, and "how much further is there to fall" IS the
late-descent question. What happened next: the gap hurt SHOCK on the log-loss screen
(+0.011 vs -0.012 calm), so the engineering pivoted to a velocity redesign
(`tgp_delta_7d`) which answers a different question — "which way is the floor
moving". The pivot was defensible on the axis it was measured on. Nobody went back
and asked whether the gap helps late descent specifically.

`tgp_delta_7d` has since been measured inert (batch0, 2026-08-19: +0.0059 c/L, 40th
percentile of the R0-vs-R0 noise floor), and its June graduation retracted. So the
velocity pivot did not rescue the series, and the strongest TGP result on record —
r2=0.63 — remains unconverted. **No TGP feature is in the lock.**

The owner's prior, which this issue exists to test: Sydney E10 troughs "kiss" the TGP
floor (overlay measured kiss-gap mean -0.3 / sd 3.1 c/L), so floor proximity should
inform exactly the descent-into-trough rows the model handles worst.

## Shape of the work

**Step 1 — fix or bound the phase axis.** Either correct the denominator for ANALYSIS
use (regime-local / COVID-break-floored, per the 2026-06-16 recipe, without
proposing it as a model feature), or re-cut the regime bands on something not built
on `mean_cycle_length` at all. Then re-run the three findings above on the corrected
axis and see whether they still disagree. They may be disagreeing because they are
binning different rows into "late descent".

**Step 2 — decide whether late descent is a target.** Only meaningful after step 1.
Deliverable is a yes/no on "is there recoverable headroom concentrated here", with
the oracle ceiling as the denominator (per feedback_oracle_ceiling_capability:
necessary, not sufficient). If the answer is no, stop — and record it, because that
closes the thread properly this time.

**Step 3 — test the gap there.** Regime-segmented, on the corrected axis, with the
shock regression treated as a known cost to be SCOPED (per
feedback_shock_gate_scoping: gate on normal-fold median + bounded shock worst-case)
rather than as an automatic disqualifier. Log-loss screen first, oracle existence
check before engineering anything PIT-safe (feedback_oracle_diagnostic_pattern).

Do NOT skip to step 3. That reproduces the June failure: a real-looking number on an
axis that cannot support it.

## Constraints that apply to any verdict here

- The realised arbiter's resolution is ~0.05 c/L per decision flip; pooled deltas
  below ~0.1 c/L are not measurements (feedback_realised_arbiter_decision_flip_quantum).
  Count differing fills before believing any pooled CPL delta.
- Grade any realised delta against the noise floor. fps-cf8 (fingerprint guard +
  atomic batch setup) should land before a NEW floor is computed, but steps 1-2 are
  diagnostic and do not need it — this issue is deliberately NOT blocked on fps-cf8.
- Candidate features go via an experiment first; features.py changes only in a
  follow-up PR (feedback_features_via_experiment_first).

## Files likely affected

- experiments/<date>_late_descent_axis/ (new experiment dir + README, per TEMPLATE.md)
- fuel_signal/cycle.py — only if step 1 concludes the production denominator must change
- experiments/ledger.yaml + INDEX.md — write both in the same pass

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The three late-descent findings are re-stated on a defensible axis, and either reconciled or one of them explicitly retracted with a reason
- [ ] A yes/no on whether recoverable headroom concentrates in late descent, measured against the oracle ceiling
- [ ] If yes: the TGP gap tested on late-descent rows specifically, log-loss screen + oracle existence check, with any realised delta graded against the noise floor and its flip count reported
- [ ] If no: thread closed in the ledger with `not_tested` naming what would reopen it
- [ ] ledger.yaml `station_minus_tgp_cents` entry updated either way — its `not_tested` currently names this exact test as the open one
- [ ] Verdict recorded regardless of outcome; a null result here is a real result given how much has been built on the "late descent is the soft spot" premise

## Related

- fps-1785999729707-1-0301bf82 (#271) — TGP production path, on hold; its scope is landing tgp_delta_7d, which is answered. Kept open as the TGP umbrella pending the owner's call.
- fps-cf8 — noise-floor fingerprint guard + atomic batch setup.
- fps-3jj.9 — the noise floor itself.

## Folded in 2026-09-02 (backlog review): fps-bqb — cycle-length drift

`fps-bqb` proposed "alert if the mean NSW cycle length drifts". It is closed as folded here
because **step 1 above already has to answer that question** — an alerting mechanism was
being filed for a drift this bead documents as measured and unfixed.

What this bead already establishes, which `fps-bqb` treated as an open hypothesis:

- `_mean_cycle_length` (`fuel_signal/cycle.py:270`) is an unweighted expanding all-history
  mean over every confirmed peak to date.
- It therefore **lags the early-2020 ~24d -> ~38d regime shift**, inflating the phase axis
  by ~13% (worse in fold 7's era).
- The 2026-06-16 `regime_cycle_length` experiment measured a regime-local replacement,
  found it genuinely more accurate (~27d -> 38d), and abandoned it because it bought no
  realised value AS A MODEL FEATURE — which says nothing about its fitness as an ANALYSIS
  AXIS, the job all three late-descent findings actually use it for.

So the drift is not in question; only what to do about it is, and that is step 1's
deliverable. Two things carried over from `fps-bqb` that step 1 should state explicitly
rather than leave implicit:

- [ ] **Name every consumer of the ~45-day constant** before changing it — `classify.py`'s
      window and `cycle.py`'s expectations at minimum — and say for each whether a corrected
      denominator would change behaviour or only change the analysis cut. This bead's
      "fix or bound the phase axis" wording currently allows an ANALYSIS-only correction;
      that is fine, but the production blast radius should be written down either way.
- [ ] **State the drift as a number over 2016-present**, not just as the ~24d -> ~38d
      break, so any later re-cut has a baseline to compare against.

Deliberately NOT carried over: the alerting/monitoring half. A recurring alert on a
quantity nothing currently reacts to is monitoring without a consumer
(`feedback_a_new_facts_field_needs_its_consumer`). If step 1 concludes the production
denominator must change, an alert becomes worth filing then — with something to alert.

Was: `fps-bqb` (P4, filed 2026-09-01 from the retired FUTURE_IDEAS.md; closed as folded).
title: Is late descent a real target, and does the TGP gap help there? Reconcile the phase axis first

description:
## What

`find_pending_runs()` (experiments/pipeline/dossier_tables.py:95) treats a run as
pending only when `results.json` exists AND `README.md` does NOT. A candidate that
was dossiered once and is then deliberately re-run — after a contract fix, say —
keeps its README, so `--scan` silently skips the new `results.json` and the run is
never dossiered.

Hit live 2026-08-19: `--scan experiments/candidates` produced no output at all for
batch0/tgp_delta_7d's third run; it had to be invoked with the positional run_dir
instead.

## Why this isn't just the documented trade-off

The function's docstring already reasons carefully about the abort-then-succeed
ordering (fps-g31) and adds the RETRYABLE_STATUSES guard for it. The
succeed-then-rerun case is the mirror image and is not covered — and it fails the
same way the docstring calls out as unacceptable: "The successful run would be
silently invisible forever."

Unattended, that means a batch re-queued after a pipeline/contract fix produces
results nobody dossiers, with no error.

## Options

- Compare mtimes: pending if `results.json` is newer than `README.md`.
- Or record the dossiered run's `git_sha`/wall in `facts.json` (it already carries
  provenance) and treat a `results.json` whose provenance differs as pending.

Second is more robust; first is one line. Either is fine — a silent skip is the
thing to remove.

## Files likely affected

- experiments/pipeline/dossier_tables.py (`find_pending_runs`)
- tests/test_dossier_tables.py

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A run dir with a README and a NEWER results.json is reported as pending
- [ ] The fps-g31 abort-then-succeed guard still holds (regression test kept)
- [ ] `uv run ruff check . && uv run pytest -q` green
title: dossier_tables --scan skips a deliberate re-run of an already-dossiered candidate

description:
## What

`process_run` calls `build_facts(run_dir)` (which reads `rowpreds.parquet`/`fills.parquet` once
for the breakdowns) and then `make_plots(run_dir, facts, batch_dir)` (which reads both again for
the plots). At fixture scale this is free; per an independent review of PR #301, real rowpreds/
fills artifacts can be multi-GB, and this runs once per candidate every night unattended.

## Why I noticed this

Partially addressed already in PR #301: `process_run` used to also re-read `results.json` a
second time just to recover `batch_dir` (now carried in `facts["provenance"]["batch_dir"]`
instead), and `_validation` used to re-read `rowpreds.parquet` a third time on top of
`build_facts`'s own read (now takes the already-loaded DataFrame). What's left is the
`build_facts`/`make_plots` split itself, which is harder to collapse without changing
`build_facts`'s public return type (a plain dict, relied on by ~15 existing tests) or adding an
optional pre-loaded-frame parameter.

## Files likely affected

- `experiments/pipeline/dossier_tables.py` (`build_facts`, `make_plots`, `process_run`)
- `tests/test_dossier_tables.py`

## Suggested fix

Something like `build_facts(run_dir, *, rowpreds=None, fills=None)` — backward compatible
(existing `build_facts(run_dir)` calls keep loading from disk), with `process_run` loading once
and threading the same DataFrames into both `build_facts` and `make_plots`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] rowpreds.parquet and fills.parquet are each read at most once per `process_run` call
- [ ] `build_facts(run_dir)` (no frames passed) still works exactly as before for existing callers/tests
title: dossier_tables.py: process_run reads rowpreds.parquet/fills.parquet twice (build_facts + make_plots)

description:
## What
The worker Routine's `bd dolt push` fails with a 403 from the session's egress proxy — confirmed as a policy restriction on Dolt's git-ref namespace, not a credential problem. This is a NEW gap, distinct from and discovered after the credential/scheme auth gap fixed in fps-ddf (which is closed and confirmed working end-to-end via PR #287).

fps-ddf fixed *authentication* (embedding a token in `sync.remote`). This gap is *network-level*: the Routine's sandboxed environment appears to allowlist egress by domain/path, and whatever path Dolt's git-remote push uses under the hood isn't on that allowlist, even though `gh` CLI calls (used for the token itself, and for opening PRs) work fine from the same environment.

## Why I noticed this
A live worker Routine run hit this while attempting `bd dolt push` after successfully reconstructing `sync.remote` per CLAUDE.md pickup rule 0. The run also caught and reverted a related side effect: `bd dolt remote add` with the token-embedded URL was about to get auto-committed verbatim into the git-tracked `.beads/config.yaml` (same trap as `bd recall bd-dolt-remote-add-auto-commits-config`, but hit here because the push failure happened after the remote had already been reconfigured). The run reverted this correctly before it landed — repo is confirmed clean, `.beads/config.yaml` has the plain untokenized URL, and `bd dolt remote list` shows a clean `git+https://` URL.

## Files likely affected
- CLAUDE.md (worker automation section, pickup rule 0 and the "Dolt remote push auth" note) — needs a new paragraph once a fix or confirmed workaround exists
- No code changes anticipated; this is an environment/policy question, likely needs the owner to check what egress allowlist governs the Routine's `environment_id` (see docs/automation.md)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Root-cause which specific host/path Dolt's git-backed push actually hits (may differ from plain `git push` to `github.com`)
- [ ] Either get that path allowlisted for the Routine's environment, or find a push path that stays within the existing allowlist
- [ ] Verify with a live triggered run that `bd dolt push` succeeds end-to-end from the Routine
- [ ] Update CLAUDE.md's worker section to document the fix (or the confirmed workaround) alongside the existing fps-ddf writeup

## Priority raised P2 -> P1 (2026-08-14, fps-3jj design session)

Different urgency from fps-6zj, and NOT a blocker for the fps-3jj pipeline — local `bd dolt push`
works fine (verified repeatedly this session), so the new local routines can write to the queue
normally. The reason to raise it is on its own merits: while push is blocked, the remote worker's
claims and closures never reach the shared Dolt DB, so its state is silently discarded every run.
That is a correctness fault in the shared queue, and it gets harder to reason about once a second
(local) consumer is writing to the same queue alongside it.
title: Worker Routine: bd dolt push blocked by egress proxy 403 on Dolt git-ref namespace

description:
## What

`tgp_delta_7d` (7-day TGP momentum) graduated from the realised/CpL arbiter in experiment `2026-06-20_leading_indicators` (Δcpl −0.039 c/L pooled, 14-fold WF). This issue covers everything needed to land it in production.

The raw gap (`station_minus_tgp_cents`) did NOT graduate: better pooled CpL (+0.097 vs vel7 alone) but it destroys vel7's gains in the expensive/high-headroom shock folds (9/10 zeroed to 0.000 from −0.299/−0.667). Ship `tgp_delta_7d` alone.

## Components

1. **AIP TGP downloader** — automated daily pull of the AIP ULP/Diesel TGP xlsx from aip.com.au. Weekday-only source; run after market close. Download URL / auth pattern to confirm. Store raw rows or parsed daily series.
2. **DB storage** — new table (or column on an existing price table) for `tgp_date / tgp_cents` (Sydney ULP TGP, c/L GST-incl). Decide normalised table vs daily parquet. Backfill from `experiments/2026-06-20_leading_indicators/data/AIP_TGP_2026-06-19.xlsx` (covers 2004→2026-06-19).
3. **`PriceHistory` TGP source** — extend `PriceHistory` (or `ModelStrategy`) with a `tgp_at(as_of)` lookup that mirrors the experiment's `.asof` semantics (ffill weekends, 1-day lag). This replaces the `extra_feature_provider` closure used in `realised_tgp.py`.
4. **`features.py` compute** — add `tgp_delta_7d` = `(tgp_today − tgp_7d_ago)` as a PIT-safe rolling column. Match `df.rolling("7D", closed="left")` (or explicit shift) as used in the experiment. No change to `FEATURE_COLUMNS` constant until the column is available in `load_features()`.
5. **`FEATURE_COLUMNS` bump** — add `"tgp_delta_7d"` to the production feature list. Regenerate `data/features.csv` / parquet cache. Re-lock the model (retrain + calibrate + write artifact) — this is a Phase bump.
6. **Backfill / gap-fill** — decide policy for weekends and public holidays (current: ffill; confirm this is correct).
7. **Tests** — PIT-lag test (tgp_at returns yesterday's value when called today), null-check on training frame, round-trip downloader test.

## Why I noticed this

Experiment `2026-06-20_leading_indicators` (arbiter run completed 2026-06-21, ~29min). The `extra_feature_provider` seam (#269) was the in-process injection path for the experiment; the lib-hoist of that seam to a first-class `PriceHistory` provider is tracked in #270 (glue hoist gated on 2nd use).

## Files likely affected

- `fuel_signal/download.py` (or new `fuel_signal/tgp.py`)
- `fuel_signal/db.py` (new table DDL + queries)
- `fuel_signal/history.py` (or `model_strategy.py`) — `tgp_at`
- `fuel_signal/features.py` — `tgp_delta_7d` column
- `data/features.csv` / parquet cache
- `data/models/lgbm*.joblib` (re-lock)
- `docs/STATUS.md` (Phase bump)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Daily TGP pull runs in CI / cron without manual intervention
- [ ] `tgp_at(as_of)` returns `None` / raises cleanly before the 2004 backfill date
- [ ] `tgp_delta_7d` column present in `load_features()` output with null rate = 0 over the live date range
- [ ] PIT lag test passes (decision date T sees TGP as of T−1)
- [ ] Model re-locked with `tgp_delta_7d` in `FEATURE_COLUMNS`; `docs/STATUS.md` updated
- [ ] `decide()` in live mode computes `tgp_delta_7d` from `PriceHistory` (not the `extra_feature_provider` closure)
title: design: AIP TGP production path for tgp_delta_7d feature graduation

description:
## What
Taking a candidate feature **derived from an external daily series** (TGP, and future: crude, FX, AIP diesel TGP) to the realised/CpL arbiter introduces a pattern the WFCV-screen lib does **not** cover: the feature must be computed at **two sites that must agree**, or you get silent train/replay skew (a leakage-class bug no test catches).

1. **Training-frame column** — `df["price_date"].map(pit_series)` (the arm's `df`).
2. **Live replay** — `ModelStrategy.extra_feature_provider` via `series.asof(pd.Timestamp(as_of))` (the #268/#269 seam).

Plus a generic PIT-align of the raw series: `series.asfreq("D").ffill().shift(lag_days)`.

First instance: `experiments/2026-06-20_leading_indicators/realised_tgp.py` (#268). Per the `experiments/lib/README.md` promotion rule (*extract on the 2nd unchanged copy*), **this is use #1** — filing the gap so the **2nd** external-series arbiter triggers the extraction, not a premature one-off hoist.

## Why I noticed this
`realised_tgp.py` PIT-aligns the xlsx (`_load_tgp_pit`) and then computes the candidate columns **twice** — once for the training frame (`.map(pit)`) and once in each live provider closure (`.asof`). The two are kept consistent by hand. A single source-of-truth helper would make drift impossible.

## Proposed API (sketch, for the 2nd-use extraction)
In a new `experiments/lib/features/external.py` (or alongside `lib/realised.py`):
- `to_pit_daily(series, lag_days=1) -> pd.Series` — `asfreq("D").ffill().shift(lag_days)`.
- `external_feature_arm(pit_series, name, *, gap_from=None) -> (add_columns_fn, provider)` — returns BOTH the training-column adder and the matching `extra_feature_provider(as_of, station_code, station_price)` from one definition, so they can't diverge. (`gap_from` handles the `station_price − level` gap arm.)

## Files likely affected
- `experiments/lib/features/external.py` (new) or `experiments/lib/realised.py`
- `experiments/lib/README.md` (document the realised-arbiter-candidate seam + when to use it)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One source-of-truth helper emits the training column AND the matching live provider.
- [ ] PIT-align transform shared, `lag_days` configurable.
- [ ] README documents the two-site consistency hazard and when to reach for this.
- [ ] **Trigger:** extract on the 2nd external-series realised arbiter; do not hoist the one-off now.
title: Hoist external-series realised-arbiter glue into experiments/lib (on 2nd use)

description:
## What
Run the realised/CpL backtest (the arbiter) on the TGP leading-indicator candidate from `experiments/2026-06-20_leading_indicators/` (#215), and decide:
1. Does `tgp_delta_7d` (7-day TGP momentum) graduate to `features.py`?
2. Does the raw gap `station_minus_tgp_cents` (R3 = gap+vel7) earn its place, or is it dead weight in low-headroom calm?

## Why I noticed this
The WFCV **log-loss screen passed**: `tgp_delta_7d` carries strong independent signal and **rescues the shock regime** where the #262 headroom map says the money is; the raw gap helps calm but hurts shock. Log-loss is a screen, not the verdict — the **realised CpL backtest is the arbiter** (memory `feedback-wfcv-logloss-screen-not-verdict`). See the experiment README for the full arc.

## Plumbing needed (production)
- **Data pipeline**: AIP Sydney ULP TGP into the feature pipeline. Source cached at `experiments/2026-06-20_leading_indicators/data/AIP_TGP_2026-06-19.xlsx` (free daily xlsx, 2004→, c/L GST-incl). Decide storage (DB table vs CSV) + a **daily refresh/downloader** (the point is it's daily-pullable alongside NSW prices).
- **features.py**: compute `tgp_delta_7d` (+ `station_minus_tgp_cents` for the R3 arm). PIT = ffill weekends + 1-day lag (or confirm same-day is safe — TGP published weekday AM).
- **backtest.py**: `PriceHistory` TGP source + `tgp_at`/velocity accessor; `ModelStrategy.decide()` adds the feature to the live vector (`_build_feature_dict` path).
- **Harness wrinkle**: `run_paired_realised_backtest` shares `feature_columns` across arms, so an *added* feature = two single-arm runs diffed (baseline vs candidate), OR extend the harness to take per-arm `feature_columns`.

## Arms
- baseline (54) vs **vel7** (55: +`tgp_delta_7d`) — primary
- baseline vs **gap+vel7** (56: R3) — does the gap convert to spend?
- score at own τ and a held τ (clean attribution); pooled CpL.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] TGP available PIT at decision time in the backtest (no leakage).
- [ ] Realised pooled CpL (own + held τ) for baseline / vel7 / gap+vel7 over the WFCV folds.
- [ ] Decision recorded; if graduating, separate PR adds to `FEATURE_COLUMNS` + flips the experiment README/INDEX status.

## Files likely affected
- fuel_signal/features.py, fuel_signal/backtest.py, fuel_signal/db.py (or a TGP loader/downloader)
- experiments/lib/realised.py (if extending for per-arm feature_columns)
title: Realised/CpL backtest for TGP velocity feature (tgp_delta_7d) — plumb + decide

description:
## What

The ±10c premium threshold in `classify.PREMIUM_BAND_CENTS` is producing cohorts too small to carry meaningful signal:

- **Sticky (>+10c premium)**: 2 stations across all of Sydney (latest scoring snapshot). 30 of 32 LGAs have zero sticky stations. Camden and Canterbury-Bankstown each have 1.
- **Discount (<-10c premium)**: 6 stations across 2 LGAs (Parramatta 4, Campbelltown 2). 30 of 32 LGAs have zero.

Per-date row-level classification is more populous (≈345 station-days where `stickiness_score < -10c` over the full history; ≈170 where `>+10c`) because the 45-day rolling window admits more transient classifications. But the per-station-persistent cohort is effectively empty.

Two issues to consider together:

**1. Threshold may be too tight.** Lowering from ±10c to ±5c would give 25 sticky / 30 discount stations (per-station latest), and bring most LGAs to ≥1. ±2c gives 97 / 126. Sensitivity to the threshold should be empirically tested — the current value was picked from "a small amount of experimentation" per user.

**2. Premium ≠ temporal stability.** The classifier in `classify.py` is purely premium-based (`median premium vs LGA cluster reference`). A station with median premium +12c above its LGA can still oscillate ±15c across the cycle — it just oscillates at +12c offset. Several downstream uses of the Sticky classification (per `project_sticky_station_exclusion` memory, and the proposed Signal B in `experiments/2026-06-06_late_descent_triplet/`) assume Sticky stations are *temporally flat baselines*, which the current definition does not guarantee.

A temporal-stability variant (low rolling std / low cycle amplitude over 45d–90d) might be a better match for the mechanism Sticky is being used for, independently of the threshold question.

## Why I noticed this

Sticky-floor reference gap is a candidate signal for late-descent regime separation (#206 / experiments/2026-06-06_late_descent_triplet). When checking whether enough sticky stations exist to build a per-LGA baseline, the coverage came back essentially empty.

Diagnostics: `experiments/2026-06-06_late_descent_triplet/step1b_sticky_coverage.py` and `step1c_discount_coverage.py` produce the threshold-sensitivity and per-LGA distribution tables cited above.

## Files likely affected

- `fuel_signal/classify.py` — `PREMIUM_BAND_CENTS` constant, classifier logic, possibly add a temporal-stability variant
- `fuel_signal/features.py` — `stickiness_score` derivation if the underlying classification changes
- LGA/brand aggregate features that exclude stickies (per `project_sticky_station_exclusion`) — re-run if the cohort definition changes
- Any downstream consumers of the Sticky/Discount class labels in `station_class`

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Document threshold sensitivity: how does the Sticky/Discount cohort size respond to ±2c, ±5c, ±7c, ±10c?
- [ ] Empirically test whether `stickiness_score` (premium-based) correlates with a temporal-stability proxy (e.g. rolling-std of station price). If correlation is weak, the two concepts are distinct and we may want both.
- [ ] Decide: lower threshold, redefine via temporal stability, or both. Justify with downstream signal use cases (#206 Signal B, sticky-station exclusion in aggregates).
- [ ] Re-run impacted aggregate features if the cohort definition changes; re-train the 50-feat Phase 4 baseline on the new aggregates.
- [ ] Update `project_sticky_station_exclusion` memory if the operational definition shifts.

## Out of scope

- Replacing the LGA cluster reference itself (still uses median across LGA stations).
- The two-pass clustering iteration logic.
title: Review Sticky/Discount classification threshold — may not be carrying signal

description:
## What

Add a per-brand level feature `brand_<slug>_premium_45d` capturing each large brand's chronic pricing strategy relative to the LGA cluster reference. Broadcast per date, one column per qualifying brand. Companion to the cycle-phase brand feature (#179), but answering a different question.

## Why

Brand-level pricing strategy is slow-moving and partially independent of cycle phase. The "tightness" of a brand's pricing desk — how aggressively it pins sites to the Competitive band vs allowing Sticky drift — varies materially across brands and across time within a single brand's tenure.

Empirical evidence (gathered while scoping the now-closed #5):

**EG Ampol sites, class share by era:**

| Era | Competitive | Sticky | Discount | Avg premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Woolworths (Jan 2018 – Mar 2019) | 99.95% | 0.02% | 0.04% | −0.03c |
| EG (Oct 2019 – Dec 2023) | 94.1% | 4.8% | 1.1% | +0.38c |

**Reddy Express sites, three regimes within one brand label:**

| Era | Competitive | Sticky | Avg premium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tight Coles (2016 – 2020-Q2) | 98.5% | 1.5% | +2.7c |
| Drifting Coles (2020-Q3 – 2023-Q4) | 92.7% | 6.8% | +2.3c |
| Viva/Reddy (2024-Q1 – 2025-Q4) | 85.9% | 13.6% | +3.3c |

Two takeaways:
1. Operator changes (Woolworths→EG; Coles→Viva) genuinely shift the brand's pricing regime — not just signage.
2. Strategy can drift within a single operator's tenure (Coles loosened ~3.5 years before Viva acquired it). A static current-brand tag can't capture this; a rolling premium statistic can.

## Why this supersedes #5

The now-closed #5 ("brand series rewrites history") proposed three options: ignore, build a brand-history table, or treat brand as a static feature. This regime-as-rolling-statistic approach is a fourth option that subsumes the original concern:

- Captures Caltex→Ampol cosmetic rebrands correctly (no regime shift visible → feature value unchanged across the transition).
- Captures Woolworths→EG genuine operator changes correctly (regime shift visible → feature value changes naturally as the rolling window crosses the transition).
- Captures within-operator strategy drift that the static-brand framing can't (e.g. Coles 2020-Q3 loosening).
- No schema change, no brand-history table, no hand-picked cutoff dates.

PIT-safe by construction (45-day window ends at `price_date − 1`, mirroring `station_class`).

## Strawman feature shape

For each qualifying brand B (using the `MIN_BRAND_SITES` threshold defined in #179):

- `brand_<slug>_premium_45d` — median over stations in B of `(station_price[t] − LGA_cluster_ref[t])` across `t ∈ [price_date − 45, price_date − 1]`
- Optional second column: dispersion of brand premium across sites (captures desk coordination vs fragmentation)

Open design question: symmetric (same value at every row for date D regardless of station brand) vs leave-one-out at brand level. Start symmetric; revisit if leakage suspected.

## Sequencing

Should land **after** #179. Two reasons:
1. Don't bundle two new brand features in a single experiment — need clean baselines to measure each independent contribution.
2. The regime feature's lift is most meaningful when measured against a model that already has the cycle-phase brand signal.

## Files likely affected

- `fuel_signal/brand_regime.py` (new)
- `fuel_signal/features.py` (broadcast `brand_<slug>_premium_45d` columns)
- `tests/test_brand_regime.py` (new)
- `tests/test_features.py`

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Per-qualifying-brand rolling premium statistic implemented, PIT-safe
- [ ] Feature columns present in `assemble_feature_rows()` output
- [ ] Test confirms PIT safety
- [ ] Test logloss reported vs baseline that includes #179's cycle-phase features
- [ ] Paired walk-forward CV vs #179-baseline with regime-segmented per-fold deltas reported
- [ ] One new row in `experiments/results.csv`
title: Brand-level regime feature: chronic pricing strategy as a level statistic

description:
## What

After Phase 3 (LightGBM) is fitted, compute the FP penalty as:

    E[damage | label=0, model predicts BUY at chosen τ]

rather than the population median across all label=0 rows.

## Why I noticed this

While choosing a grounded FP penalty (fp_cost.py diagnostic, PR #57), three views were considered:
- Population median (5.80c) — current choice, frequency-weighted across all label=0 rows
- Cluster B median (9c) — costs when a real drop was imminent
- Model-conditional — damage distribution over rows the fitted model actually misfires on

The model-conditional view is the most principled because the FP penalty should reflect what the model gets wrong, not the full label=0 population. A model that preferentially misfires on cluster A (expensive-but-stable) days has a near-zero true FP cost; one that misfires on cluster B (drop was coming) days has a ~9c cost.

## Files likely affected

- `fuel_signal/fp_cost.py` — extend `compute_damage` or add a new function that takes fitted model + features CSV, runs predict_proba, filters to FP rows at a given τ, and reports the damage distribution
- `fuel_signal/score_phase2.py` (or equivalent Phase 3 scorer) — may want to log model-conditional FP cost alongside standard metrics

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For a fitted ML model and a chosen τ, compute damage distribution over label=0 rows where model predicts BUY
- [ ] Report mean, median, p25/p75/p90 — same format as fp_cost.py summary table
- [ ] Compare to population median to quantify how much the model's misfires skew toward A vs B
- [ ] Use result to decide whether 5.80c remains appropriate or should be revised
title: Revisit FP penalty using model-conditional damage distribution (View 3)

description:
## What
The two-condition BUY label uses a percentile gate on the past-90-day price distribution to catch high-price plateaus:

\`\`\`python
label = 1 (BUY) if:
    future_min >= today_price - threshold   # no better deal coming in next H days
    AND today_price <= Nth percentile of past 90 days  # price is cheap in absolute terms
\`\`\`

The percentile threshold N is currently set to 33rd as a starting point. It hasn't been tuned.

## Why revisit
- 33rd percentile → ~15 cheap days per 45-day cycle
- 25th percentile → ~11 cheap days per 45-day cycle
- The right value is whichever threshold best aligns with "genuinely good buying opportunity" validated against the backtest
- Changing N changes the label definition, which changes the training set, which changes the model — so this is a design decision not a free knob

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Run labels with N=25, 33, and at least one other value (e.g. 40)
- [ ] For each: inspect the positive rate and distribution of BUY days across the cycle
- [ ] Validate against backtest: which value produces the best simulated purchasing outcomes?
- [ ] Document the chosen value and rationale in `labels.py` docstring
- [ ] Consider whether forward horizon H (currently 7d) should also be revisited at the same time (14d was floated as an alternative to better handle plateaus)
title: Tune label percentile hyperparameter (25th vs 33rd vs other)

description:
## Background

Current data pipeline captures E10 only in snapshots and the DB. Historical CSVs contain all fuel types (diesel, U91, premium unleaded, LPG, etc.).

## Hypothesis

Non-E10 price series may carry predictive signal for the E10 cycle:

- **Diesel** is priced off a different commodity (gasoil vs gasoline), but retail margin pressure may propagate across fuel types at the same station. A diesel price drop may lead an E10 drop at the same site.
- **U91 vs E10 spread** may widen/compress at different cycle phases — the spread itself could be a feature.
- **Premium unleaded** follows E10 closely with a roughly fixed premium; deviations from that premium may flag retailer behaviour changes.

## What's needed

1. Load non-E10 prices into the DB (historical CSVs already have them; snapshot pipeline needs to be extended or a separate ingestion path added).
2. Build per-fuel daily series helpers (existing `get_daily_prices` is already fuel-code-agnostic).
3. Evaluate cross-fuel features in Phase 3 of the ML plan (lightgbm + station/cross-station features).

## Scope note

This is a feature-engineering task for the ML model, not an inspect workbench addition. The workbench can expose non-E10 series later as a side-effect once the DB has the data.
title: Add non-E10 fuel types as ML signal features

description:
## Background

`data/snapshots/` CSVs are a bridge — collected daily by GH Actions — until the NSW bulk historical CSVs cover the same period. The goal is to keep the committed snapshot count as small as possible.

## Trigger

When a new bulk historical CSV is released that overlaps any date already in `data/snapshots/`.

## Steps

1. Identify which snapshot dates the new CSV covers.
2. Compare prices per station/date between snapshot and historical CSV. Current policy (`INSERT OR IGNORE` with snapshots loaded first) means **snapshot prices win silently** — verify this is correct before retiring.
3. If prices agree (within acceptable tolerance): delete the retired snapshot CSVs from the repo.
4. If prices diverge: investigate before retiring — divergence reveals something about the data (e.g. different rollup time, intraday vs end-of-day difference).

## Open questions to resolve at first overlap

- The historical CSV rollup time is unknown. Compare against snapshot collection time (currently ~10:00 UTC = 8pm AEST / 9pm AEDT) to see how well they align.
- If they diverge materially, reconsider whether snapshot-wins is the right conflict policy — historical CSVs may aggregate the day's data differently.

## Notes

- This cannot be fully validated until the first overlap occurs (snapshots started 2026-04-27; no historical CSV covers this yet).
- Don't add more snapshot retention logic until this workflow is validated at least once.
title: Snapshot retirement: verify and delete snapshots once historical CSVs cover the same period

`--batch-dir` / `--candidate` / `--bead-id`. So a launch-queued candidate is
always a five-station run, and wide runs are hand-invoked only.

**Deliberately deferred, not overlooked.** The omission produces the CORRECT

design decision, not plumbing, and nothing currently wants it: the owner is
not trying to support wide runs at this stage (2026-09-06).

## Why it is P4

Only worth doing if wide runs stop being a supervised, hand-run job and start
being queue work. Until then hand invocation is the right interface, and a
width policy invented ahead of a need would be guesswork.

## Related

`fps-3jj.22` — the other "wide candidates need instrument work" item.

NOTE: fps-3jj.22's description and title were STALE (they described a
`placebo.MAX_RULER_ARITY = 3` cap removed by fps-3jj.25, and the title stated the
inverse of current behaviour). **Both corrected 2026-09-06** — no action needed.

- experiments/pipeline/launch.py (`build_runner_cmd`)
- tests/test_launch.py

description:
## CURRENT STATE (corrected 2026-09-06 — read this before the history below)

**There is no arity cap. `placebo.MAX_RULER_ARITY` does not exist.** It was removed by
fps-3jj.25 on 2026-08-26; the "SCOPE CHANGED" section near the bottom of this description
has said so since that day, but the opening paragraph still asserted the cap as live and
contradicted it. Corrected here so `bd show`'s lead is the truth.

What is actually true today:

- **`screen_draw_groups` has no arity limit.** The only bound is physical — a draw needs
  `arity` distinct source columns, so arity cannot exceed the usable baseline column count
  (~49 of 54; 5 `days_since_trough_entry_<lga>` are all-NaN).
- **Reuse is PRICED, not forbidden.** `placebo.effective_n_draws` converts source-column
  overlap into an effective draw count that `family_wise_z_threshold` consumes, so a wide
  candidate gets a wider, harder bar instead of no verdict.
- **`reason_code: floor_arity_below_run` is LIVE, but it is not this.** Do not conflate the
  two arity refusals (`dossier_tables.py:141` and `:159`):
  - `NOISE_BAND_REFUSAL_ARITY = "floor_arity_below_run"` — **live.** Means the FLOOR is
    narrower than the run; the fix is to compute a wider floor, and it is deliberately
    carved out of dossier.md's default `outcome: rejected` for exactly that reason.
  - `RETIRED_NOISE_BAND_REFUSAL_ARITY_CAP = "run_arity_above_cap"` — **retired**, and this
    is the one that was about the cap. Named in code only so a stale `facts.json` carrying
    it stays recognisable.
- **`TEXTURE_ICC_BOUND = 0.274`**, not the 0.391 the table below is computed at (fps-3jj.23,
  PR #338). The NOTES on this bead carry the re-priced figures; the table is kept because it
  is self-labelled and the pigeonhole argument it illustrates is unchanged.

**Live confirmation, 2026-09-06 (fps-ajs):** a 410-station floor was computed at arity 1 and
correctly refused all five batch1 candidates with `floor_arity_below_run` (they are arity 2
and 3); an arity-3 floor was then run at the same width and cost the SAME wall clock, because
the fit loop is per DRAW, not per column (`noise_floor.py:409`). Arity is free in time and
costs only resolution: 40 draws x arity 3 needs 120 column-slots from 49, giving ~28.1
effective draws and a `z_gate` of 1.7332 against arity 1's 1.7058 — 0.027 of a bar.

## What remains open

Drawing placebo source columns from OUTSIDE `LOCKED_FEATURE_COLUMNS` would reduce overlap and
**tighten** the bar for a wide candidate. That is an optimisation worth ~0.001 c/L at arity 3
and ~0.074 c/L at arity 35 (see NOTES) — three orders under the realised arbiter's decision
quantum at the widths `docs/routines/generator.md` actually invites. Nothing is blocked on it.

## Why no sampling rule can lift it

A draw needs `arity` DISTINCT source columns and only ~49 of the 54 locked columns are usable
(5 `days_since_trough_entry_<lga>` columns are all-NaN). So as arity rises, draws are forced to
overlap — and it is a pigeonhole limit, not a sampler defect: **two 35-column draws taken from
49 columns must share at least 21 of them.** Measured exposure of a 20-draw bank
(`experiments/2026-08-26_placebo_draw_independence/`):

| arity | picks | draw pairs sharing a column | effective draws @ ICC 0.391 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 60 | 5.8% | 14.0 |
| 4 | 80 | 16.3% | 9.0 |
| 5 | 100 | 27.9% | 6.5 |
| 10 | 200 | ~100% | 2.4 |
| 35 | 700 | 100% | 2.4 |

Two placebos from the same source column share that column's TEXTURE exactly — same values,
same NaN pattern, only re-dated — which correlates their deltas, shrinks the band's sample std
and makes the bar too EASY. That is the bias direction fps-3jj.14 exists to remove, arriving by
a different door. A band above the cap is still COMPUTABLE; it just is not a ruler.

## Why this matters

`docs/routines/generator.md` justifies multi-column candidates on the 35 LGA event features
having gone in together. **That precedent is gradeable now** — fps-3jj.25 made any arity
gradeable by pricing reuse; a 35-column per-LGA candidate builds a 20-draw bank on batch1's
real frame and grades at -0.287 c/L. (This paragraph previously read "still ungradeable",
true when filed and false since 2026-08-26.) What remains is that a wide candidate carries a
harder bar than a narrow one — correctly so, and by a small amount at the live ICC.

## Options

1. **Non-model computed columns.** `features.NON_MODEL_COLUMNS` holds evaluated-and-rejected
   series (brand trough columns, TGP expressions). Real features with real texture, and
   excluded from the lock so a placebo built from one is not a near-copy of a baseline column.
   Cheapest; needs a count — is there enough of it to matter?
2. **Synthetic series with matched texture.** Preserves distinctness without limit, but needs a
   defensible "matched texture" rule, and a synthetic placebo is a weaker analogue of a real
   candidate. fps-awz already rejected white noise for exactly this reason (trees ignore it,
   giving a band too NARROW and a gate too permissive).
3. ~~**Accept the cap and say so in generator.md.**~~ **MOOT** — there is no cap to accept.
   What generator.md could still usefully state is the arity/bar tradeoff, not a limit.

## Depends on

`fps-3jj.23` — **DONE** (2026-08-27, PR #338). Measured by column: point estimate 0, one-sided
95% upper bound **0.274** (down from 0.391), design resolvable to 0.262. The bound is what
grades, so this bead was demoted rather than closed — see NOTES. The table above is still
quoted at the old 0.391 and is therefore pessimistic.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision recorded on which option, with the source pool's size stated
- [ ] ~~`MAX_RULER_ARITY` re-derived~~ **MOOT** — the constant is gone. The replacement
      question is whether the effective-draw penalty at the target arity is worth reducing,
      priced with `experiments/2026-08-27_texture_icc/power.py` before any building
- [ ] `docs/routines/generator.md` states the arity/bar tradeoff (there is no range to state)


## Update 2026-08-26 (PR #335 review)

The cap shipped at **3, not 4**. It was 4 on a comparison that does not survive symmetrising:
"today's ruler" was scored 8.33 effective draws by charging its seed-collision pair a DELTA
correlation of 1.0 guessed from a COLUMN correlation of 0.965, while reuse was charged the
measured 0.391 delta-space bound. Score both alike (9.27), or against the post-fix ruler that
actually exists now (10.00), and arity 4 (9.04) stops clearing. Arity 3 (13.98) clears all three.

So this bead's scope is slightly larger than filed: it is now the route above **3**, not above 4,
and the first thing to check is whether fps-3jj.23 alone lifts the cap back to 4+ without any
outside-the-lock work at all. At the ICC point estimate (~0) every arity in the table sits at
20.00 effective draws.

## SCOPE CHANGED 2026-08-26 by fps-3jj.25 — this is no longer a precondition

The title said "the only route to a high-arity band" and that stopped being true the same day.
`MAX_RULER_ARITY` is **gone**: source-column reuse is priced into the threshold by
`placebo.effective_n_draws`, so a wide candidate is **graded**, not refused. A 35-column
per-LGA candidate builds a 20-draw bank on batch1's real frame and grades at **-0.287 c/L**.

What survives is the physical fact, and it is now an OPTIMISATION rather than a blocker: two
35-column draws from 49 usable columns must overlap in >= 21 of them by pigeonhole, so a wide
bank genuinely is worth fewer effective draws and genuinely does carry a harder bar (3.23
effective draws at arity 35, against 20.00 at arity 1-2). Drawing placebo sources from outside
the lock would reduce that overlap and **tighten** the bar — worth having, not needed to unblock
anything.

**Dropped to P3 at the time, and check fps-3jj.23 first.** (Now **P4**, per the NOTES' own recommendation after fps-3jj.23 reported.) The bar on a wide candidate is currently set by
`TEXTURE_ICC_BOUND = 0.391`, a pessimistic upper bound whose point estimate is ~0. If
fps-3jj.23 measures the ICC near zero, every width collapses to the arity-1 bar and this bead
buys nothing at all. Measure before building.
notes:
## Re-triaged on fps-3jj.23's result, 2026-08-27 — DEMOTED, not closed.

The texture ICC was measured by column: point estimate 0, one-sided 95% upper bound **0.274**
(down from the 0.391 bound this bead was sized against), design resolvable to 0.262.
`placebo.TEXTURE_ICC_BOUND = 0.274` since PR #338.

fps-3jj.23's rule was "close this if the ICC is near zero, because then overlap costs nothing".
The POINT ESTIMATE says exactly that. The BOUND does not, and the bound is what grades — so
this is not a close.

**What it can still buy, at the live constant:**

  arity 3   0.001 c/L      arity 20  0.033 c/L
  arity 10  0.013 c/L      arity 35  0.074 c/L   (was 0.135 at icc 0.391)

So the ceiling roughly halved, and it is only reachable by candidates far wider than anything
batch1 has run (its five were arity 1 and 3). At the widths docs/routines/generator.md actually
invites, this bead is worth ~0.001 c/L — three orders under the realised arbiter's decision
quantum.

**And it is no longer the cheapest route to that 0.074.** Drawing placebo sources from outside
the lock changes the null's CONSTRUCTION; taking more draws does not. The 0.274 is limited by
the design's resolution, not by anything about the data — 12 columns x 5 seeds (60 draws,
~11.4h) lands near 0.23 even if the point estimate again comes out at 0, and nearer 0.15 if F
comes in below 1 again as it did here. experiments/2026-08-27_texture_icc/power.py prices any
shape in seconds.

**Recommendation: drop to P4 and do nothing until a wide candidate actually needs the bar
tightened — at which point re-measure the ICC first, since that is cheaper and less invasive
than changing what the null draws from.**
## Title and lead corrected 2026-09-06 (fps-ajs)

The title read "...get an easier placebo bar — tighten it if one is ever proposed". That was
true when filed and INVERTED since fps-3jj.25: reuse is now priced by
`placebo.effective_n_draws`, which LOWERS the effective draw count and RAISES the bar. Measured
on the live constant: arity 1 at 40 draws is n_eff 40.00 -> z_gate 1.7058; arity 3 at 40 draws
is n_eff 28.08 -> z_gate 1.7332. Wide candidates are graded conservatively, not leniently, so
there is no leniency left to "tighten" — the open work is the opposite, SHRINKING a penalty
that is currently pessimistic (it rests on TEXTURE_ICC_BOUND = 0.274 whose point estimate is 0).

This mattered more than a normal stale field because `bd ready`/`bd list` show the title only,
so the inverted claim was the only thing a triage pass would ever see.
title: Wide (high-arity) candidates pay an effective-draw penalty — shrink it (placebo sources outside the lock) if one is ever proposed

description:
## What
`fuel_signal/dates.py` has three small pure functions with zero dedicated test coverage:
- `date_to_int(s: str) -> int` — '2024-01-15' → 20240115
- `date_from_int(v: int) -> str` — 20240115 → '2024-01-15'
- `int_to_date(v: int) -> date` — 20240115 → date(2024, 1, 15)

Add a `tests/test_dates.py` covering normal cases and the round-trip
(`date_from_int(date_to_int(s)) == s`, `int_to_date(date_to_int(s)) == date.fromisoformat(s)`).

## Why I noticed this
Scanning for trivial worker-validation tasks; every other module in `fuel_signal/` has a matching
`tests/test_*.py` file except `calibrate`, `compare`, `config`, `dates`, `label_inspect`,
`label_viz`, `stations` — of those, `dates.py` is the only one that's pure functions with no I/O,
DB, or plotting dependency, making it the cleanest, lowest-ambiguity coverage gap to close.

## Files likely affected
- tests/test_dates.py (new file)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] tests/test_dates.py exists and exercises date_to_int, date_from_int, int_to_date
- [ ] Covers at least one round-trip assertion between date_to_int and date_from_int/int_to_date
- [ ] uv run pytest -q passes
title: Add unit tests for fuel_signal/dates.py

## What
Two experiment lab-book READMEs contain relative links of the form `[#195](../../../../issues/195)`
that resolve outside the repo and 404 — they need to become plain GitHub issue URLs instead.

Files and lines:
- `experiments/redundancy_phase4b/README.md:20` — `[#195](../../../../issues/195)`
- `experiments/2026-06-03_drop_redundant_pair/README.md:159,170,173,176,178,181,184` — links to
  issues #195, #191 (x2), #194 (x2), #193, #192

## Why I noticed this
Scanning the repo for trivial worker-validation tasks; ran a link-checker over every `.md` file's
relative links and these were the only broken ones repo-wide. GitHub Issues were retired in favour
of Beads (see AGENTS.md § Beads), so these paths can never resolve locally or on GitHub as relative
links — they need to be absolute URLs: `https://github.com/edwinsteele/fuel-price-signal/issues/<N>`.

## Files likely affected
- experiments/redundancy_phase4b/README.md
- experiments/2026-06-03_drop_redundant_pair/README.md

title: Fix broken relative GitHub issue links in old experiment READMEs

close_reason: Low-value design follow-up; tolerating the fixed 3-date regression check for now
description:
## What
signal-regression.yml (design-labeled PRs only) currently checks signal output at 3 fixed --as-of dates (2025-06-01, 2025-12-01, latest). Now that it restores the full-history db-* cache (2016-08-01 onward, kept fresh daily by daily-db-update.yml — see PR #281), it could check a much wider spread of dates/regimes instead of 3 fixed points, giving a more comprehensive regression signal.

## Why I noticed this
Came up while wiring the daily DB update trigger — the user pointed out the cached DB could support more comprehensive CI. PR #281 did the mechanical cache swap only; this issue is the follow-up design question of which dates/regimes to actually check and how to present a wider diff without a noisy PR comment.

## Files likely affected
- .github/workflows/signal-regression.yml

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Decide a representative spread of --as-of dates/regimes (e.g. one per identified cycle regime/shock period, or a systematic stride across history) rather than 3 arbitrary fixed dates
- [ ] Keep the PR comment readable (full-history diff could get long — may need summarization/truncation)
- [ ] Runtime stays reasonable for a PR-blocking check
title: Broaden signal-regression.yml date/regime coverage
